stem: Which cloud provider offers the Azure platform?
explanation: Azure is Microsoft's public cloud platform. Amazon runs AWS, Google runs Google Cloud, and Oracle runs its own Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.

stem: Which cloud deployment model shares a provider's infrastructure among many unrelated customers over the internet?
explanation: A public cloud is multi-tenant infrastructure that a provider sells to any customer. A private cloud serves one organization, a hybrid cloud combines private and public resources, and on-premises infrastructure is owned and run in the organization's own facility.

stem: Which storage type keeps data as items in a flat namespace, each with a unique key and its own metadata?
explanation: Object storage holds each item with a key and metadata in a flat bucket rather than a folder tree. Block storage exposes raw fixed-size blocks, file storage uses a hierarchy of folders, and local storage is simply a disk attached to one machine.

stem: What does a container package together so that an application runs the same way on any host?

options.text: A full guest operating system and virtual hardware
The host's kernel and its device drivers
The application and its runtime libraries

explanation: A container bundles the application with its libraries, runtime and settings while sharing the host's kernel. A virtual machine carries a full guest operating system, source code alone lacks dependencies, and containers do not include the host kernel or drivers.

stem: Which storage type uses a dedicated network to give servers block-level access to shared disk arrays?
explanation: A SAN is a dedicated network that gives servers block-level access to shared disks. NAS shares files over the regular network, an object store is accessed by key through an API, and a local drive is attached to a single machine.

stem: A team saves analysis files to a NAS device on the office network. Which storage type are they using?
explanation: NAS is a network device that shares files and folders with many users, so it is shared file storage. It is not attached to one machine as a block device, it is not a cloud object service, and it persists data on disk rather than in RAM.

stem: A hospital keeps patient records in its own data center but runs seasonal reporting workloads on a public provider, with both environments connected. Which model is this?
explanation: Combining connected on-premises or private resources with public cloud services is a hybrid cloud. Public alone would move the records off-site, private alone would exclude the public provider, and a community cloud is shared by organizations with common needs.

stem: A bank must keep full control of hardware and data location but wants self-service provisioning for its analysts. Which model fits best?
explanation: A private cloud gives cloud-style self-service on infrastructure dedicated to and controlled by one organization. Public cloud and multicloud place data on providers' hardware, and hybrid puts some workloads on public infrastructure.

stem: An analyst must archive millions of image files and serve them to a web application at low cost. Which storage type fits best?
explanation: Object storage scales cheaply to huge numbers of unstructured files and is accessed by web address or API. Block storage is costly and tied to a server, local storage cannot be shared at scale, and file shares struggle with very large flat collections served to the web.

stem: A database server needs a volume with low latency for frequent small random writes. Which storage type is the usual choice?
explanation: Block storage lets the database read and write individual blocks with low latency, which suits transactional workloads. Object storage rewrites whole objects, archive tiers are slow to retrieve, and file shares add protocol overhead and locking.

stem: An analyst's Python script works on her laptop but fails on a colleague's machine because of library version differences. What best solves this?

options.text: Move the script to a larger server
Store the script in object storage
Run the script in a container
Email the colleague the script again

explanation: A container image fixes the runtime and library versions, so the script behaves the same everywhere. A larger server, a different storage location or resending the file leaves the version mismatch in place.

stem: Compared with virtual machines, what is the main reason containers start faster and use fewer resources?

options.text: They share the host operating system kernel
They store all their data in object storage
They compile applications into machine code

explanation: Containers share the host kernel instead of booting a guest operating system, so they are lightweight. They run on virtual or physical hosts alike, their storage choice does not drive startup time, and they do not compile code.

stem: An analyst keeps an extract on her laptop's internal drive. What is the main drawback of this local storage?

options.text: It has higher latency than a network share
It requires an internet connection to read
It cannot store image or video files
Others cannot easily access or back it up

explanation: Local storage is tied to one device, so sharing and central backup are hard and the data is lost if the device fails. It is usually faster than network storage, works offline, and can hold any kind of file.

stem: A company buys servers for its own data center instead of renting cloud capacity. Which cost pattern does it take on?
explanation: On-premises hardware is bought upfront as a capital expense, and the company also runs and maintains it. Pay-per-use, per-query and subscription billing are cloud consumption models.

stem: A retailer's on-premises reporting server runs at 20% most of the year but is overloaded for two weeks each holiday season. Which approach handles the peak most cost-effectively?

options.text: Buy enough servers on-premises to cover the peak
Move all reporting into a private cloud
Shut off reporting during the holiday weeks
Burst the extra load to public cloud resources

explanation: Cloud bursting is a hybrid pattern that rents public capacity only while it is needed. Buying for the peak leaves hardware idle most of the year, a private cloud still needs owned capacity for the peak, and shutting off reporting fails the business.

stem: Several analytics servers must mount the same set of folders, edit files in place and keep standard file permissions. Which storage fits best?

options.text: A block volume on one server

explanation: A shared file system lets many hosts mount one folder tree, edit files in place and honor file permissions. Objects are replaced whole rather than edited, a block volume normally attaches to one server at a time, and local disks are not shared.

stem: A company runs dozens of containerized ETL jobs that must restart on failure and scale with load across a cluster. What does it need?

options.text: A NAS device for the job files
A VPN to the cloud provider

explanation: A container orchestration platform schedules containers across a cluster, restarts failed ones and scales them with demand. A bigger single virtual machine is still one point of failure, a NAS device only stores files, and a VPN only secures the network link.

stem: Which TWO of the following are major public cloud providers?
explanation: AWS and Google Cloud sell public cloud infrastructure and services. Tableau is business intelligence software, pandas is a Python library, and MySQL Workbench is a database client tool.

stem: Which TWO are typical advantages of public cloud over on-premises infrastructure?

options.text: Full physical control of the hardware
Rapid scaling up or down on demand
Access that works without a network connection
Paying only for capacity actually used
Lower cost for steady, heavy workloads

explanation: Public cloud offers elastic scaling and consumption-based pricing. Physical control is an on-premises trait, cloud access depends on the network, and steady heavy workloads can cost more in the cloud.

stem: Which TWO statements describe benefits of containerization for analytics workloads?

options.text: Each container boots its own full operating system
Containers store persistent data inside the image
Workloads move easily between cloud and on-premises
Containers are tied to the provider that built them

explanation: Containers give a reproducible environment and are portable across on-premises and any cloud. They share the host kernel rather than booting an operating system, keep persistent data in external volumes rather than the image, and are not tied to the provider that built them.

stem: Which TWO storage options can be shared by multiple servers over a network?

options.text: A flash drive plugged into one server

explanation: NAS shares files and a SAN shares block volumes over a network. An internal drive, a flash drive in one server and a RAM disk are local to a single machine.

stem: A company needs analysts in three regions to read the same raw data lake files and wants storage to grow without capacity planning. Which THREE object storage traits meet these needs?

options.text: Access by key through a web API
Rich metadata stored with each item
In-place edits of a few bytes in a file
Mounting as a boot volume for servers

explanation: Object storage scales almost without limit, is reached by key through an API from any region, and stores custom metadata with each object. It replaces whole objects instead of editing bytes in place, and low-latency transactions and boot volumes need block storage.

stem: The diagram shows a company's analytics infrastructure. Label each unlabeled box.
explanation: An owned data center linked to a public provider forms a hybrid setup: the data center is on-premises, shared folders for many users sit on NAS file storage, and raw files addressed by key sit in cloud object storage. Block storage is a raw volume for a single server, not a shared folder tree or keyed files.

partExplanations.z-dc: Hardware the company owns and runs in its own facility is on-premises.
partExplanations.z-share: NAS shares a folder hierarchy with many users over the network.
partExplanations.z-bucket: Object storage holds items in a flat namespace addressed by key.

stem: Sort each description into the storage type it describes.

items.text: Files are reached by key through a web API
Data is organized in a hierarchy of folders and paths
A raw volume that a server formats with its own file system
Cheap, near-unlimited capacity for a data lake
The disk a virtual machine boots from

explanation: Object storage uses keys, a web API and a flat namespace that scales cheaply. File storage uses folders and paths. Block storage gives raw volumes, such as a virtual machine's boot disk, that the server formats itself.

partExplanations.meta: Access by key through a web API defines object storage.
partExplanations.tree: A folder and path hierarchy is file storage.
partExplanations.volume: An unformatted raw volume is block storage.
partExplanations.archive: Data lakes usually sit on low-cost, highly scalable object storage.
partExplanations.san: A boot disk is a raw block volume attached to the virtual machine.

stem: Match each scenario to the infrastructure model it describes.

prompts.text: A startup rents all its servers from Azure and pays by the hour
A defense contractor runs an internal portal where teams spin up their own virtual servers on its hardware
A clinic keeps records in its own server room and backs them up to Google Cloud
A factory runs its database on servers it bought and keeps on site, with no cloud tooling

explanation: Renting shared provider capacity is public cloud, dedicated self-service infrastructure is private cloud, combining owned and public resources is hybrid, and owned servers without cloud features are traditional on-premises.

partExplanations.p1: Pay-as-you-go capacity from a provider such as Azure is public cloud.
partExplanations.p2: Cloud-style self-service on the company's own hardware is a private cloud.
partExplanations.p3: Owned infrastructure combined with a public provider is hybrid.
partExplanations.p4: Owned servers on site with no self-service layer are traditional on-premises.

stem: Pinewood Analytics is moving a Python forecasting job to the cloud. The job must run identically in testing and production, read years of raw sensor files cheaply, and write results to a transactional database. Configure the deployment.

fields.label: How to package the forecasting job

options.text: Script copied from an analyst's laptop
Script stored on a NAS share

fields.label: Storage for the raw sensor files

options.text: Local disk on the job host

explanation: A container image makes the job reproducible across environments, object storage holds large raw archives cheaply, and block storage gives the database low-latency volumes. A copied or shared script does not pin dependencies, local disks vanish with the host, and file or object storage add latency for transactional writes.

partExplanations.runtime: Pinned libraries in a container image give identical runs in testing and production.
partExplanations.raw: Object storage is the low-cost, scalable home for years of raw files.
partExplanations.db: Databases need the low-latency random access of block storage.
